name: Alice's Adventures in Permuting
description: Alice mixed up the words transmutation and permutation! She has an array $$$a$$$ specified via three integers $$$n$$$, $$$b$$$, $$$c$$$: the array $$$a$$$ has length $$$n$$$ and is given via $$$a_i = b\cdot (i - 1) + c$$$ for $$$1\le i\le n$$$. For example, if $$$n=3$$$, $$$b=2$$$, and $$$c=1$$$, then $$$a=[2 \cdot 0 + 1, 2 \cdot 1 + 1, 2 \cdot 2 + 1] = [1, 3, 5]$$$. Now, Alice really enjoys permutations of $$$[0, \ldots, n-1]$$$$$$^{\text{∗}}$$$ and would like to transform $$$a$$$ into a permutation. In one operation, Alice replaces the maximum element of $$$a$$$ with the $$$\operatorname{MEX}$$$$$$^{\text{†}}$$$ of $$$a$$$. If there are multiple maximum elements in $$$a$$$, Alice chooses the leftmost one to replace. Can you help Alice figure out how many operations she has to do for $$$a$$$ to become a permutation for the first time? If it is impossible, you should report it. $$$^{\text{∗}}$$$A permutation of length $$$n$$$ is an array consisting of $$$n$$$ distinct integers from $$$0$$$ to $$$n-1$$$ in arbitrary order. Please note, this is slightly different from the usual definition of a permutation. For example, $$$[1,2,0,4,3]$$$ is a permutation, but $$$[0,1,1]$$$ is not a permutation ($$$1$$$ appears twice in the array), and $$$[0,2,3]$$$ is also not a permutation ($$$n=3$$$ but there is $$$3$$$ in the array). $$$^{\text{†}}$$$The $$$\operatorname{MEX}$$$ of an array is the smallest non-negative integer that does not belong to the array. For example, the $$$\operatorname{MEX}$$$ of $$$[0, 3, 1, 3]$$$ is $$$2$$$ and the $$$\operatorname{MEX}$$$ of $$$[5]$$$ is $$$0$$$.
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10^5$$$). The description of the test cases follows. The only line of each test case contains three integers $$$n$$$, $$$b$$$, $$$c$$$ ($$$1\le n\le 10^{18}$$$; $$$0\le b$$$, $$$c\le 10^{18}$$$) — the parameters of the array.
output_specification: For each test case, if the array can never become a permutation, output $$$-1$$$. Otherwise, output the minimum number of operations for the array to become a permutation.
approach_summary: Verify predicate monotonicity: P(x) is true for x ≤ K and false otherwise. Binary search over the answer domain to find the boundary in O(log(Range) × Verify_Time).

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 2028B — Alice's Adventures in Permuting [33. Binary Search]
topic_editorial.summary: Binary search on the monotonic answer domain.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The predicate function $P(x)$ ('Is answer $\le x$ feasible?') is monotonic: if $P(x)$ is true for some value, it remains true for all larger values (or vice versa). This allows binary division of the answer search space $[\text{low}, \text{high}]$ in $O(\log(\text{Range}))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N \log(\text{Range}))$
  The binary search divides the search interval by 2 at each iteration, requiring $\log_2(\text{Range})$ steps. In each step, the feasibility check `check(mid)` scans the array in $\mathcal{O}(N)$ time.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(1)$ auxiliary space
  The algorithm operates directly over the input array without allocating extra auxiliary memory.
